notes.title: Devblog #8
notes.content:
Hello everyone!

Today is Wednesday, and I'd like to talk about one of the last mechanics of the game, along with the enemy type they are mostly tied with!

Let's start!

[h1]A Literally Ground Breaking Mechanic[/h1]

Let’s kick things off with a quick introduction to one of the core mechanics: [b]the breaking ground[/b].

This feature was one of the first ideas I had when designing the game, but I initially struggled to find a creative way to integrate it into the [b]Tower[/b]. 
In the early zones, its role was filled by the spikes, which I'll leave for you to discover while playing.

However, the breaking ground finally found its perfect role in the [b]game’s fourth zone[/b]. 
Since this part of the game is set underground, it made much more thematic sense.

At first, I imagined Shorty falling into an endless void, but visually, that turned out to be pretty boring, given the camera of the game. 
Then, during a break, I stumbled upon some videos inspired by the “[b]the floor is lava[/b]” challenge. It instantly clicked, this was the [b]visual hook[/b] I was looking for!

In essence, the ground collapses shortly after you pass over it, revealing a lava pit underneath. Very few elements in the game can survive on it, adding a fresh layer of danger and urgency to your movement.

[h1]The Cobolds[/h1]

And that’s where the [b]Cobolds[/b] come in!

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45527515/9307553da9139948f7a4efe32f9024da2ed84006.png[/img]

Right after I implemented the breaking ground mechanic, I started working on these enemies. 
At first, I actually imagined them with wings, so much so that, in the game files, they’re still called "[b]flying_enemy[/b]".

The problem? The winged design I envisioned [b]didn’t fit within the pixel grid[/b] constraints. 
So, wings had to go, but the idea stuck.

Lorewise, if you're curious, you’ll learn more about them on Saturday, but from a gameplay perspective, [b]they’re the only enemies that can walk on lava[/b].

This adds a whole new layer of challenge to the breaking ground mechanic. 
Players now [b]need to think twice[/b] about every step, because [b]Cobolds[/b] might still be lurking, ready to intercept, [b]whether there’s lava or not![/b]

[h1]The Design[/h1]

From a level design standpoint, they have inspired some of my personal favorite levels: what I call the "[b]labyrinth levels[/b]".

These are [b]convoluted mazes[/b] of breaking ground tiles, sometimes mixed with Cobolds and additional mechanics to push your movement strategy even further.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45527515/818b1ae453f3386fd778a0ffb9be2ea8979d105b.png[/img]

As for their visual design, I leaned into the idea of [b]warrior miners[/b]. 
It ties perfectly into their lore, and I wanted their weapons to reflect that too. 
They wield fierce [b]pickaxes[/b] and massive [b]hammers[/b] in one hand, because yes, they’re that strong!

I hope you enjoyed this small behind the scenes look at one of the game’s unique mechanics and its enemies!

Have a great day and look out for cracks on the floor!
-Giuseppe

notes.title: Devblog #7
notes.content:
Good afternoon!

This wednesday, I'll introduce to one of the late enemies of the game: [b]the Moleoids![/b]

What makes them unique, and what differentiates them from similiar enemies?
Let's take a look!

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45527515/014476b83fe4a9eebf7ee691fdb495fde2f87fb6.png[/img]
(they are still work in progress, of course. I think I should position them better on the tile...)

The "Moleoids" were created to fulfill a specific need: [b]enemies capable of avoiding traps[/b].
Some might argue that dwarves already serve this purpose, but from a strictly technical standpoint, that's not quite accurate.

[b]Dwarves can avoid obstacles[/b], but if an obstacle is placed directly in their path, [b]they are forced to stop.[/b]
[b]Moleoids, on the other hand, are not.[/b]
If they need to go underground, they will; [b]nothing stops them![/b]
[b]The only way[/b] to block them is to [b]place an obstacle exactly where they resurface[/b].
Otherwise, there’s nothing that can truly halt them!

They also have a [b]particularly interesting trait[/b]: when a Moleoid is underground, [b]the player can stand on the same tile as them![/b]

However, this comes with a caveat.
[b]While underground[/b], Talpoids are completely [b]immune[/b] to any offensive actions from King Shorty.

From a level design perspective, implementing them turned out to be more interesting, and less difficult, than I had initially expected.

The only real challenge was communicating how this mechanic works to the player.
Unlike regular enemies, [b]an underground Moleoid is hard to spot and visually track.[/b]

The solution being implemented is to show a [b]small mound of dirt[/b] on the tile where the Moleoid is burrowed. 
This mound will be designed to clearly stand out from the surrounding tileset, with special handling in edge cases, for example: if the surface tile is already occupied by a crate, the mound won’t appear, [b]but the tile will still look slightly darker than normal ones.[/b]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45527515/52e819e4e209a1bcaee566cef8417e83bf03464c.png[/img]
There are 2 Moleoids in this image. One is under the chest (with a darker black, as always WIP), the other one is under the tile below (the arrow is there just for the screenshot.)

(The mound of dirt has not been implemented yet, as I'm not yet satisfied with how it looks, so nothing to show!)

[h1]Design[/h1]

Initially, much like the dwarves, [b]Moleoids were quite different.[/b]

They were meant to follow custom paths in each level, [b]carrying oversized bombs that would explode every few tiles.[/b]

Although the idea was intriguing, [b]I ultimately decided not to implement it[/b], for three main reasons, one more critical than the others:

[olist]
[*] [b]There wasn’t much thematic connection between moles and bombs.[/b] (This could've been addressed by tweaking the design, but explosions didn’t feel quite right in a fantasy/medieval setting anyway.)

[*] [b]The bomb mechanic took up too much space in the levels[/b], significantly complicating navigation and making level design a nightmare. The bombs would also destroy every element in the environment, further increasing complexity. (While this could have been managed by refining the mechanic and making compromises, I felt it would’ve resulted in a gameplay element that lacked identity and inspiration.)

[*][b] It was extremely difficult to clearly communicate both the mechanic and the enemy[/b]. In a game like this, where planning your moves is essential and in which the player relies heavily on being able to predict enemy movements and trap behavior, [b]having a mechanic that changed enemy movement in every level made this predictability impossible[/b], undermining one of the core pillars of the game’s design.
[/olist]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45527515/31aac346098f9039a064909511969ca13ebdeaf9.png[/img]

In the end, I decided to focus the Moleoids on being [b]"trap/obstacle-evading"[/b] enemies, setting aside the explosive concept, at least for now.
It might be an idea worth revisiting in the future.

So...
That’s all for today!
Hope you enjoyed this devblog and found it interesting.

-Giuseppe

notes.title: Devblog #6.5
notes.content:
Hello everyone,

today is, once again, Saturday.

As always I'd like to remind you that this ".5" blogs are focusing just on the lore of the game.
If you are not interested, come next week to discover a new enemy type!

With that out of the way, let's start!

Here in Italy, summer has slammed the closing doors of spring, and as such... [i][b]it's damn hot outside![/b][/i]

That's the reason for the choice of this devblog, in which I'll tell you something about people that hate hot temperatures... [b]Dwarves![/b]

[h1]Map: The Dwarven Skaldom[/h1]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45527515/43564314b27f44e2771052f19521f7e0935cbbbb.png[/img]

[h1]The Origins[/h1]

The roots of the dwarven people are cloaked in mystery.
The only surviving account of their ancient history comes from the [b]Manual of Western Races[/b], written by an anonymous monk of the [b]Eastern Thunder Order[/b]:

[list]
[*] [i]“Long ago, Dwarves were grotesque beings born deep beneath the earth, shaped from blood and mud by the will of a forgotten god. All they knew was battle.
When that god vanished, leaving behind only strange remnants scattered across the world, the Elves had already become a powerful and advanced race. Yet even they were caught off guard by the relentless advance of a mysterious bearded folk, who began landing on their shores shortly after the god's disappearance.”[/i]
[/list]

Sadly, elven records were lost to time, and this passage is all that the greatest scholars of the East have managed to recover from the few surviving documents spared by the Living Hell.

[h1]Modern History[/h1]

Before the rise of [b]Skal the Immortal[/b], the dwarves lived in isolated mountain clans.
Each clan ruled its own mountain, and serious conflict only broke out in the gravest of disputes.

Everything changed when a young dwarf, whose name would one day become legend, discovered an ancient arcane tome at the base of [b]Mount Sumnia[/b].

Some believe this book predates even the formation of dwarven civilization, written when they were still muddy, shapeless creatures, but no one knows for sure. 
Skal has never allowed a single soul, not even his own offspring, to lay eyes on it.

What is known is this: Skal grew older, fathered countless children with countless dwarf-women... and [b]outlived them all[/b].
Indeed, Skal has buried every one of his children, 24 generations of dwarves have come and gone.
[b]That’s several millennia[/b], by dwarven standards.

In time, [b]Skal became something greater than a ruler.[/b]
He is now revered more than the ancient gods, those remembered and those long lost. 
To all dwarves, he is the one true sovereign. Hence, the monarch of the [b]Dwarven Skaldom[/b].

He led his people beyond the mountains, founding thriving cities throughout the [b]Coldlands[/b] and the [b]Wallwoods[/b].

It might sound like the tale of a wise and ageless king. 
And it is.
But that’s only part of the truth...

[h1]Skal the Mindbender[/h1]

Skal exercises direct mental control over every dwarf in his realm.
Only [b]a rare few[/b] manage to [b]resist[/b] his [b]influence[/b], and those who do [b]are hunted down like beasts.[/b]

Refugees speak of an overwhelming compulsion to return to their homeland, haunted by a single, obsessive thought before breaking free:
[b]Serve Skal.[/b]

[h1]Moments of Freedom[/h1]

According to scholars who study mind control, Skal may be using an ancient elven spell, once described in texts now lost to the Living Hell.
Escaped dwarves, however, insist in saying the true source of his power is the book, Skal’s book.

According to them, it also... "suggests" to him ancient sacrificing rituals to extend his life.
(Some say that Skal kills his own offspring to live eternally, but it has never been witnessed.)

Interestingly, the mind control isn’t constant.
There are moments when his grip weakens, especially in two notable situations:

[h1]The High Jump Tournament[/h1]

Skal is a passionate fan of [b]high jump competitions.[/b]
For a dwarf, he is said to be exceptionally tall, and this might explain his unusual fascination with the sport.

Despite his incredible age, Skal always ranks first.
His score is in the thousands.

For perspective: [b]each tournament grants the winner just one point.[/b]
[b]And they’re held once per year.[/b]
Considering the average dwarf lives around 350 years... it’s practically impossible to reach such numbers, unless, of course, you’re Skal.

When a tournament is held, however, Skal control isn't as strong as the rest of the year, maybe because he is too busy focusing on the sport.

[h1]The Beardserkers[/h1]

There exists a special group of dwarves who are almost entirely free from Skal’s mental hold:
[b]the Beardserkers[/b], elite dwarven warriors trained in the arcane art of teleportation ([b]the only form of magic allowed in the Skaldom[/b]).

Every newborn is personally examined by Skal for signs of magical potential.
If any is detected, the child is taken from their family and sent to train in the [b]Beardserkers’ Pines[/b].

There, from the age of one, they undergo brutal daily training: plunging into icy waters, lifting impossible weights, and harmonizing with nature, all to master the teleportation art for warfare.

Dwarves are typically slow and sturdy.
Beardserkers [b]are the exception[/b].
They’re as fast as lightning (by dwarven standards), teleporting behind enemy lines to strike with lethal precision.

They also serve as Skal’s preferred invasion force, and also as collectors of debts.
(As Gnomia learned firsthand during the reign of King Shorty.)

[h1]Sworn Enemies of the Dwarves[/h1]

For generations, the [b]Dwarven Skaldom[/b] ruled the western lands under Skal’s iron mind.
That era ended with the sudden invasion of the [b]Fishmen[/b] from the North.

The attack came without warning, not even Skal’s prophetic abilities foresaw it.
Caught unprepared, he was forced to redirect the full might of his armies northward, ultimately abandoning many vassal kingdoms.

[b]The Miningdom of Coboldia[/b] and [b]The Molearchy[/b] were lost.

Skal attempted to hold onto [b]Gnomia[/b], considered a strategically vital location, but, well... we all know how that ended.
(And if you don’t, go and read [b]Devblog #2.5[/b])

To this day, the Fishmen remain a real threat.
Though the borders are now stable, their strength lies in their diversity: each fishman is unique, with its own abilities and traits.
[b]This makes it extremely difficult for Skal to devise a single, effective offensive strategy.[/b]

[h1]Business Sense[/h1]

Still, [b]war is no excuse to neglect the economy[/b]. Skal knows this well.

Dwarves are master artisans of [b]Runesmithing[/b] and [b]Stonecrafting[/b].
Any respectable ruler hires dwarves when there’s stonework to be done.

Shorty, or rather, his aunt, might have a thing or two to say about that...
But I’ll let you uncover that story on your own directly in game!

That’s all for now
[b]Have a nice day and may your jumps reach ever higher![/b]

-Giuseppe

notes.title: Devblog #5
notes.content:
Hello everyone,

This Wednesday's update is a bit different: instead of talking about an enemy type, I want to focus on the core design of the game: 
how the genre choices were made, the challenges I faced, and the solutions I came up with.

Let’s get started!

[h1]Why Turns in a Puzzle Game?[/h1]

This decision dates back to the earliest stages of development, when the game was just a concept for a gamejam.

I wanted to blend several genres in a meaningful way, while preserving the key elements of each one of them:
[list]
[*] [b]Puzzles: Every move should be deliberate[/b]. The game is best played when the player thinks ahead, since each action has[b] predictable outcomes.[/b] I hope that solving tricky situations or escaping seemingly impossible blocks gives that satisfying [b]“I got it!” moment.[/b]

[*] [b]Turn-based[/b]: The idea of [b]"turn economy"[/b] forces the player to think strategically within a limited number of moves. Ideally, this leads to decision making like: “How can I make the most of this level? Should I move there and perform that action, or do the opposite?”

[*][b] Dungeon Crawler[/b]: This comes from my nostalgia for old games of this type that I played as a kid. Reaching the stairs at the end of a level always made me wonder: [b]What’s next? What new enemies or mechanics will I encounter?[/b]
[/list]

[h1]The Challenges[/h1]

The biggest challenge has been [b]balancing all of these elements[/b]. Specifically:
[list]
[*] Some puzzles risk of being [b]too complex or too simple[/b]. I want players to think through their actions, but not to face overly convoluted logics or feel like they’re just ticking off obvious boxes from a visual checkbox.

[*] [b]Turns can feel too restrictive[/b]. It’s frustrating to almost finish a level, solving everything correctly, only to be killed by the turn limit.

[*] [b]The sense of discovery needs to be preserved throughout the game[/b]. Facing the same enemies repeatedly gets dull. How often should I introduce new mechanics? Will they stay fun? Should each enemy feel distinct?
[/list]

[h1]The Solutions I’ve Found[/h1]

[list]
[*] Given that players have different problem-solving styles, [b]I focused on gradually introducing mechanics[/b]. This helps players understand what they can and can’t do. If they carefully plan their moves, and study the level, they should be able to resolves the various challenges they'll face in not so many attempts.
I hope that it works well. 
Some levels also allow for multiple solutions, so I had to balance the turn limits accordingly to keep them challenging no matter the chosen path.

[*] The “big brain move” regarding the turn limit was adding an easier difficulty mode, because this game lends itself well to that. [b]This way people that want to take a more relaxed approach can.[/b] 
But honestly, it felt a bit cheap. 
I’d rather players finish levels in the main difficulty. So what was the answer? 
Designing levels that gradually introduce challenges. [b]Every level has its set of obstacles that are generally divided in sections (for example a room or a corridor)[/b]. If players solve each challenge correctly, they should finish with the right number of turns.

[*] To maintain engagement, I’ve aimed to [b]introduce[/b] at least one [b]new mechanic[/b] or simple, well designed [b]enemy types[/b], [b]every few levels[/b] (on average, every 4 levels, with some exceptions).
It was important that they [b]felt unique and meaningful.[/b]
[/list]

[h1]The Influence on the Narrative[/h1]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45527515/c45d88c4e85a411a831f8ff4c7a73f1d021694b9.png[/img]

[b]I wanted the mechanics to be tied into the story[/b]. So, throughout the game, there are [b]in-universe explanations[/b] for how the systems work.

For example, the turn system is the result of a spell cast by Archmage Tip (named so because he gives tips, ahahaha). 
Other game mechanics like coins, traps, and even the dialogue system are similarly [b]woven into the narrative[/b].

This approach, I believe, [b]makes the game more immersive and “self-aware”[/b], adding a subtle but meaningful layer of engagement. Given the lighthearted and comedic tone of the game, I think this integration was the right call.

That’s all for today, I hope you found this devblog interesting!

I Wish you all a great day!
-Giuseppe

notes.title: Devblog #4
notes.content:
Hello everyone,

Today I'll tell you something about the first race I've [b]NOT[/b] designed around the mechanic of the sunlight: [b]the Imps![/b]

[h1]Why Imps?[/h1]

During the development of the game I realized that in certain situations, during the creation of the levels, I was blocked with some technical limitations that were, apparently, impossible to avoid.
They were inherited by the design of the original enemies, which move every turn.

One of these problems was that, at a certain point of the game, I wanted to create "tunnels" of two tiles each, [b]or even less[/b], with enemies that guarded them.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45527515/471c349d905a325115350f71c1d1ce9bf7571497.png[/img]

The problem was obvius.
Given that enemies move by one tile each turn, it was impossible for Shorty to get through these areas.
So, whats the solution?

[h1]Let Them Sleep![/h1]

It came to me while solving a rare bug, in which enemies [b]could not move for a turn.[/b]
Fortunately the bug was resolved quickly, but everytime it happened I tought it would be a nice mechanic to attach to an enemy.

For this very reason I created the Imps, that everytime they move they must rest for 1 turn, allowing players to move even through the narrowest of spaces, [b]IF they think carefully about their turns![/b]

[h1]The Design[/h1]

The sleep mechanic initially was explained only with text, using the dialogues of the game.

However, after many tests, I've realized that sometimes it wasn't clear wheter an Imp was sleeping or moving.
[b]This problem was especially obvious when there was a level that had an imp after many levels in which there weren't.[/b]

Because of that, I've added them a [b]unique animation that triggers only when they sleep[/b], along with a particle effect: [b]the very very classical "ZzZzZzZZzzz...".[/b]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45527515/22bb5038e4691afbc9837894c78150d26ad536e2.png[/img]

(TRIVIA: it is the same effect that its used for the stun effect of the goblin, just with another sprite!)

[h1]The Consequences[/h1]

The peculiarity of imps is that they are usually positioned in order to be a nuisance.
If, apparently, avoiding them is very simple, they can make the players lose a lot of turns, if they took too much time to arrive to the point in which one is present.

[b]Waiting for an imp to move, means that Shorty will lose double the turns![/b]

Additionally, I've found interesting that, if they are placed along with other enemies, imps give an unexpected complexity to the level they are in.

[b]The player is infact forced to align their "mental route", with two different movement times.[/b]
This is an important challenge in terms of level design, that in my opinion needs to be discussed along the theme of "timing".

Given that the imp is a type of enemy that is encountered in the later stages of the game, the player should be already quite familiar with the game rhythm.
The presence of an enemy that moves one tile every two turns, breaks this rhythm, altering the gameplay with a slowdown.

Others enemies of the game behave similiarly, Dwarves for example, that will be talked about in the following weeks.
These type of enemies, [b]that "break the rhythm"[/b], are, in my opinion, a foundamental addition to the game, that throw in a [b]more varied gameplay[/b], and new challenges that do not alter greatly the foundation of the game.

Also, there is another enemy type which belongs to the Imp race, but I'll leave it for you to discover.

I hope you liked this devblog, and I'll take this chance to remember you that tomorrow (29/05/2025) the [b]game demo will be realeased![/b]

I hope you will like it!
May you sleep as peacefully as do the Imps!

-Giuseppe

notes.title: Devblog #1
notes.content:
Happy Wednesday, everyone!

Today marks the first time I’m sharing a bit about the game’s mechanics, so I thought I’d start from the very beginning, with the main game idea and the first enemy type I implemented: [b]Goblins![/b]

[h1]The Theme and the Idea[/h1]

When I first came up with "Will The King Escape?", I was partecipating in the [b]Godot Wild Jam #66[/b].
I had a few days to create a short game and there was a main theme to follow, along with optional “wildcards” suggesting mechanics to include.

The main theme was [b]"escape"[/b], which later inspired the game's title and the gameplay loop, and one of the wildcard mechanics was [b]"sunlight"[/b]. 
That optional card immediately got me thinking about a system that would encourage more interaction between the player and the environment.

The only problem? I didn’t have a game yet to build that mechanic into!

[h1]The Game and the Goblins Origin[/h1]

I decided to create a turn-based system where both the player and the enemies take 1 turn to move. The peculiarity was that enemies follow predefined paths, acting as obstacles to the player escape. 
This made level complexity emerge naturally from the number and placement of enemies, and since their path was predetermined, it was like a [b]pathfinding puzzle![/b]

To add an extra level of difficulty, I've also added a turn limit in which the King is forced to reach the stairs.
This way the player must carefully think about every action, in order to make the best of each turn.

[h3]The First Invaders[/h3]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45527515/da1af65d1ee97103d0c056336298f966607ef287.png[/img]

The first enemies I designed and implemented were [b]Goblins[/b]. 
As an avid fantasy fan, it just felt instinctive!
They also happened to match well with the Tower tileset I had created, which is designed on a small 32x32 pixel grid. 
Since goblins are typically small creatures, they fit perfectly within that scale.

[h3]The Sunlight[/h3]

The sunlight mechanic came shortly after: opening windows to [b]stun or block[/b] enemies, creating opportunities for the player to forge new, previously hidden, paths.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45527515/2252ade878936e7047e518ef0aaa90b6557cc692.png[/img]

To make this interaction clearer, I visually linked the windows with bright [b]yellow[/b] (an infamous color that unironically fits the game very well) [b]cords[/b] to help the connection stand out.

However, after testing some levels, I realized that sunlight could be a [b]double-edged sword[/b]: sometimes players could accidentally trap themselves!
So in later levels, for example, I added scenarios where you need to close windows instead, in order to reopen a viable escape path. It added a simple and nice layer of puzzle-solving.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45527515/fc2fb543f0a2374738db3c4fbf64a9f4a4a9b29f.png[/img]

Also, to introduce the player to the mechanic in a way that felt more organic, I've decided to create a few levels with very simple windows, which are always open (in other words: [b]these don't have a curtain[/b]).

There are more sunlight-related mechanics in the game (as you may have seen in the trailer or read about on the Steam page), but since they involve other enemies in the Tower, I’ll cover those in future devblogs. 
So if you enjoy behind the scenes insights, be sure not to miss any updates!
(Shameless self-promotion: complete.)

[h3]What about the Story of these Goblins?[/h3]

If you're curious about the Goblins themselves, their background and quirky habits (which influenced their design), make sure to check out Saturday’s post! 
I’ll be sharing their territory map and I'll dive into their culture, including why they really can’t stand the sun!

Have a great day,
Until next time!

-Giuseppe

Also, to introduce the player to the mechanic in a way that felt more organic, I've decided to create a few levels with very simple windows, which are always open (in other words: these don't have a curtain).
